title: The Destruction of the Library of Alexandria

beats.label: HOOK
beats.narration: Before you believe the caliph burned the Library of Alexandria, know the story has zero evidence from the century it happened in. The real story isn't one fire — it's a three-hundred-year death with at least three different suspects, and the most famous one probably never touched a single scroll.

beats.label: THE TURN
beats.narration: Today we're tracing what actually happened to the Library of Alexandria — what's solid, what historians still argue about, and the one popular version that's almost certainly a myth.

beats.label: BEAT 1 — The founding
beats.narration: The Library was part of the Mouseion, a research institution founded in the early Ptolemaic dynasty, in Egypt. Tradition credits Demetrius of Phalerum with proposing it to Ptolemy I — though some historians call his exact role debatable, so treat that detail as likely, not certain.

beats.label: BEAT 2 — How big was it, really
beats.narration: Nobody knows exactly how many scrolls it held. Estimates range from 40,000 to as high as 700,000 — but that top figure comes from ancient writers centuries later, and modern historians consider it almost certainly exaggerated.

beats.label: BEAT 3 — Caesar's fire, 48 BCE
beats.narration: The most commonly blamed culprit. Caesar's own account only mentions burning ships and docks — it's a later writer, Strabo, writing twenty-five years afterward, who connects the fire to the library. Historians still dispute how much was actually lost, and there's evidence the library kept functioning afterward.

beats.label: BEAT 4 — The Serapeum, 391 CE
beats.tag: SOLID temple destruction / UNCERTAIN library link
beats.narration: In 391 CE, the Serapeum temple in Alexandria was destroyed under Bishop Theophilus — that part is well documented by near-contemporary writers. What's not documented: any ancient source actually connecting that destruction to a library collection still existing at the time. The two events get merged in popular retellings. The sources don't support that merge.

beats.label: BEAT 5 — The caliph myth, 641 CE
beats.narration: The most famous version — a caliph ordering the library burned because its books were either redundant with or contrary to the Quran — traces to a single writer, Bar Hebraeus, writing roughly six hundred years after the fact. No source from the century it supposedly happened mentions it. And the same exact story gets told about a different library, under the same caliph, somewhere else entirely — a strong sign it's a reused legend, not a record.

beats.label: PAYOFF
beats.narration: So the Library of Alexandria wasn't destroyed. It was worn down — a fire here, a purge there, a temple demolition that got conflated with it later, across three centuries — and the single-villain version everyone repeats is the one part of the story with the least evidence behind it.
